interest: A drunk U.S. sailor and the Japanese flag at Tsingtao, 1935.
overview: This file (classified under State Department decimal file 894.015311 and cross-referenced with 811.30 Asiatic Fleet) documents a diplomatic incident that occurred in Tsingtao (Qingdao), China, in October 1935. On the night of October 17, 1935—the Japanese memorial day commemorating soldiers killed in the 1914 Siege of Tsingtao—an intoxicated American sailor from U.S. Asiatic Fleet Submarine Squadron Five mishandled and dislodged Japanese flags. The incident triggered immediate outrage among the local Japanese community, culminating in a hostile crowd of approximately 500 Japanese civilians menacing American naval officers and Consul Samuel Sokobin. Japanese consular officials demanded formal apologies at the Japanese Consulate General, punishment of the sailor, and assurances of non-recurrence, while the local Japanese press published inflammatory accounts linking the matter to recent tensions in Chefoo. Through coordinated diplomacy between Consul Sokobin, Commander Sherwood Picking, and a Japanese naval intelligence officer, the dispute was resolved without formal public humiliation through expressions of regret and a cordial, symbolic visit at the Japanese Consul General's private residence.

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the Japanese flag incident in Tsingtao, subsequent consular protests and mob hostility, and American diplomatic responses.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin reports that a drunk American sailor interfered with Japanese flags at Tsingtao on October 17, 1935, provoking a crowd of 500. He expressed regret but declined a formal apology at the Japanese Consulate.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Sokobin (Tsingtao) on Japanese flag incident and demands for apology
